subtype: College sleep debt and mood swings [Actor]
passage: I'm Vidya, and I share Room 214 in the hostel with Ayesha. This term she has lived on late-night chai and videos in bed, then slept through her morning lectures. Last week she snapped at me for asking about the laundry, then sat on her bed staring at nothing. On Friday she said, "I just feel flat. Maybe I need a new study app, or one of those morning-routine videos." I didn't know what was going on inside her, so I only said, "You've barely slept all week." She looked surprised, as if she hadn't connected the two. Since Sunday she has set one alarm for the same time every day and put the kettle away at night. She's laughing at my jokes again, though I can't say for sure that's why.

qa.q: What did Ayesha snap at Vidya for?
qa.a: For asking about the laundry.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling on Friday, and what did she think would fix it?
qa.a: She felt flat and low, and thought a new study app or morning-routine videos might help, without linking her mood to sleep.

qa.q: Which change seems to have helped, and why?
qa.a: A steady alarm time and putting the kettle away at night; small, regular sleep changes seem to lift her mood more than a motivation trick would.

qa.q: How is Vidya affected by Ayesha's sleepless weeks?
qa.a: Vidya gets snapped at over small things and is unsure what is going on inside Ayesha, but cares enough to point out the missing sleep.

grounding: Shows a hostel student running on late nights and chai, feeling flat and snappy without linking it to sleep, and small sleep changes helping.

subtype: College sleep debt and mood swings [Actor]
passage:
Week one: Jahnavi stayed up with the corridor gang till the small hours, drank cup after cup of cutting chai and skipped the early lab. By evening she was jittery, and she cried over a message from Ojas that only said "ok".
Week three: Ojas found her half asleep in the library. "You're not lazy, you're exhausted. Try one thing: the same wake-up every day, even Sunday." Jahnavi grumbled but set the alarm.
Week six: She still stays up late some nights, but she wakes at the same time and has stopped napping through the afternoon. The "ok" messages don't sting anymore. She told Ojas she feels steadier than any productivity video ever made her.

qa.q: What did Ojas's message say in week one?
qa.a: It only said "ok".

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi cry over the short message?
qa.a: She was exhausted and jittery, so she felt hurt and anxious over something small that would not bother her when rested.

qa.q: What small step did Jahnavi try, and why did it help?
qa.a: Waking at the same time every day, even Sunday; a steady rhythm eased her sleep debt and steadied her mood.

qa.q: How does Ojas see Jahnavi's struggles in week three?
qa.a: Ojas sees exhaustion, not laziness, and offers one simple change instead of a lecture.

grounding: Illustrates a college student's late nights, chai and skipped classes bringing jittery, teary moods, and one regular sleep habit lifting them over weeks.

subtype: Roommate living with a night owl [Receiver]
passage:
Last semester, sharing a PG room with Sarita nearly broke me. She's a night owl: laptop glow, calls with her cousins abroad long after midnight, the kettle clicking. I said nothing. Instead I sighed loudly, left sticky notes like "Some of us have class in the morning :)" and banged my cupboard at dawn. She started ignoring me back. A silent war in a room the size of a shoebox. Then one night, lying awake and furious, I realised she might not even know how much it bothered me. Next morning I said it plainly: "The light and the calls late at night wake me up. Could you take calls in the common room and turn the desk lamp to the wall? I'll get an eye mask." She said sure, and sorry. I wish I'd said it in the first week.
Parveen

qa.q: Where did Parveen ask Sarita to take the calls?
qa.a: In the common room.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling while leaving the sticky notes?
qa.a: Parveen felt resentful and annoyed but said nothing directly, so the anger leaked out as sighs, notes and banging.

qa.q: What finally worked, and why?
qa.a: Naming the problem plainly with a specific request and offering a compromise; Sarita could fix what she finally understood.

qa.q: How might the sticky notes have looked to Sarita?
qa.a: Like sarcastic jabs rather than a clear request, which is why she started ignoring Parveen back.

grounding: Shows a roommate kept awake by light and late calls turning passive-aggressive, then ending the quiet feud with a clear request and a compromise.

subtype: Roommate living with a night owl [Receiver]
passage: Warden's note, Girls' Hostel, Block C. Over two weeks I have seen small signs between Sabina and her roommate Gargi in room 108: Sabina sleeping on the common-room sofa twice, the two eating at separate tables, a note on their door reading "QUIET HOURS EXIST". Today Sabina came to my office, eyes puffy. Gargi edits videos and takes calls late into the night; Sabina has early practicals and has barely slept. She admitted she had been slamming drawers instead of saying anything. I suggested she speak soon, before it hardens into a feud, and helped her plan one clear request. This evening, with me present, Sabina asked for headphones and for calls on the balcony after lights-out. Gargi agreed and asked to keep a small desk lamp on, facing away. Sabina will try an eye mask. I will check in with both on Monday.

qa.q: What did the note on the door say?
qa.a: "QUIET HOURS EXIST".

qa.q: How was Sabina feeling when she came to the office?
qa.a: She was worn out and upset, eyes puffy, and resentful enough that she had been slamming drawers instead of talking.

qa.q: What did the warden do that helped, and why?
qa.a: The warden encouraged Sabina to speak early, helped plan one clear request and sat in on the talk, so a quiet feud became a fair deal.

qa.q: How might Gargi have experienced the weeks before the talk?
qa.a: Gargi probably felt the chill of separate tables and a pointed door note without any clear request to act on.

grounding: Illustrates a roommate whose sleep is broken by late calls and light growing resentful, and an early, specific request with a compromise stopping the feud.

passage: At the Andheri office, Nilesh wore his short nights like a medal. "Sleep is for after the promotion," he joked by the coffee machine, refilling his mug yet again. In the client review he cut Lalit off twice and snapped, "Can we move faster?" Then Lalit pointed at the screen: the totals in Nilesh's sheet were off by a whole column. The room went quiet. Back at his desk, Nilesh's hands were jittery. He scrolled back through the week: a wrong date in an email, a missed call, a sharp reply to the intern. All since the late nights began. That evening he shut his laptop early and left it in the office drawer.

qa.q: What was wrong with Nilesh's sheet?
qa.a: The totals were off by a whole column.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling back at his desk?
qa.a: He felt shaken and embarrassed, with jittery hands, as he saw his slips had piled up since the late nights began.

qa.q: What could Nilesh keep doing, and why?
qa.a: Protecting his sleep, as he started to by leaving the laptop at the office, since rest would sharpen the judgment his late nights were wearing down.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt when Nilesh cut in twice?
qa.a: Lalit was likely irritated at being cut off, yet still pointed out the error that mattered.

grounding: Shows a young professional treating short sleep as dedication, then seeing poorer judgment, irritability and leaning on coffee lower his work.

passage:
Subject: A confession, and a question

Dear Arnab,
You once told our class that the best architects protect their mornings. I laughed. In my first year at the firm I slept as little as I could and called it commitment. I answered client mail after midnight and was proud of my red eyes.
Lately it has gone wrong. Last week I approved a drawing with a staircase that went nowhere. In meetings I bite people's heads off, then spend the evening apologising. I lean on coffee all day and still feel foggy. The hours were meant to make me better at this, and they are making me worse.
I have started small: phone off at night, a proper breakfast, no email in bed. Did you ever go through this? How did you learn to leave work at a sane hour without feeling lazy?
Warmly,
Zeenat

qa.q: What was wrong with the drawing Zeenat approved?
qa.a: It had a staircase that went nowhere.

qa.q: How does Zeenat feel about the long hours now?
qa.a: Zeenat feels worried and let down, realising the hours meant to prove commitment are making the work worse.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's first steps seem sensible, and what else could help?
qa.a: Phone off at night, a proper breakfast and no email in bed are good starts; talking with a manager about workload could help too.

qa.q: How might Arnab react to this email?
qa.a: Arnab might feel concerned but not surprised, having once warned about protecting mornings, and glad to be asked.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who treated little sleep as commitment now noticing mistakes, irritability in meetings and reliance on coffee.

passage: Gautam, you asked why I, Jagdish, never join the gossip about who's slipping. Years ago at the bank, a sharp young officer called Rukmini began making small mistakes: a wrong date on a draft, a customer's name misspelt twice. Her jokes went flat, and she snapped at the peon over a file. Others whispered that she had lost interest. I was tempted to mark her errors in red for the manager. Instead I asked her for tea on the terrace and said, "You're not yourself lately. Is the workload too much? Are you getting any rest?" She went quiet, then told me her mother was ill and she had spent most nights at the hospital. I helped her ask the manager to move the heavy files for a while. A quiet question did more than a red pen ever could.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish invite Rukmini for tea?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: What was Jagdish tempted to do, and what feeling lay behind it?
qa.a: Jagdish felt irritated by the repeated mistakes and was tempted to mark them in red for the manager.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Choosing a private, kind check-in over tea instead of reporting the errors; it revealed the hospital nights and led to a lighter load.

qa.q: How might the whispering have felt to Rukmini if she had heard it?
qa.a: Unfair and lonely, since she was exhausted from hospital nights, not uninterested.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing small errors, flat humour and sharpness in a usually sharp teammate and choosing a private, kind check-in over criticism.

passage: With the pitch due by afternoon and the air conditioning broken, the Chennai studio was hot and cranky. Jaya noticed that Shalini, usually the quickest wit on the team, had sent the wrong file twice and misspelt the client's name on slide three. When Kiran joked about it, Shalini just said, "Fine. Fix it yourself," and turned back to her screen. Someone muttered, "What's up with her lately?" Jaya had a pile of tasks of her own. Still, she caught Shalini at the water cooler. "No pressure, but you've seemed really wiped out this week. Too much on? Are you sleeping?" Shalini's shoulders dropped. "Barely. The Mumbai project has me up past midnight." Jaya fixed slide three herself and, after the pitch, went with Shalini to ask their lead about sharing out the Mumbai work.

qa.q: What did Shalini misspell on slide three?
qa.a: The client's name.

qa.q: What does Jaya's decision to stop, despite her own pile of tasks, suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt concerned for Shalini, enough to set aside her own pressure for a private check-in.

qa.q: What worked about Jaya's approach, and what might have gone wrong otherwise?
qa.a: Asking privately and kindly about workload and sleep uncovered the cause; joining the muttering would have left Shalini defensive and still exhausted.

qa.q: What was the day like for Shalini before Jaya asked?
qa.a: Probably miserable: worn out, making slips, then teased about them, so she snapped.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague under deadline pressure noticing a drained teammate's errors and flat humour and checking in privately about workload and rest.

subtype: Persistent insomnia and knowing when to seek help [Response]
passage:
"You're up again," Hemant said, finding his wife Jyoti on the balcony.
"I did everything right. No phone in bed, same wake-up time, no tea after lunch. And I'm still staring at the ceiling."
"How long has this been going on?"
"Weeks. And it's not just the sleep. Everything feels grey. I cried on the metro yesterday over nothing."
"Jyo, that's not something to push through alone."
"I keep thinking I should just try harder."
"You have tried hard. Maybe it's time to see Dr Sen. Not instead of your routine, alongside it."
"What if she says it's nothing?"
"Then we'll know. And if it's something, we'll know that too."
Jyoti leaned against him. "Okay. I'll call the clinic in the morning."
"I'll come with you."

qa.q: Where did Jyoti cry yesterday?
qa.a: On the metro.

qa.q: What is Jyoti worried about when she hesitates?
qa.a: She is anxious that the doctor will say it is nothing, and she feels she should just try harder.

qa.q: Which choice is wise here, and why?
qa.a: Calling the clinic while keeping her routine, because weeks of poor sleep with a grey mood call for a doctor's help, not more pushing through.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Jyoti's efforts?
qa.a: He sees she has already tried hard, so he treats seeing the doctor as the sensible next step and offers to go with her.

grounding: Shows someone whose sleep stays poor for weeks despite good habits, with low mood, choosing to see a doctor while keeping the routine.

subtype: Persistent insomnia and knowing when to seek help [Response]
passage: Last winter I thought I could fix my sleep like a spreadsheet. Blackout curtains, the same alarm every morning, no screens in bed, a warm drink. For weeks I lay awake anyway, my mind looping over work and my dad's retirement money. I started dreading bedtime. My friend Simran listened on a video call and said quietly, "Sabina, you've done all the right things. This is the point where you tell a doctor." I was embarrassed, as if needing help meant failing. But I booked an appointment. The doctor asked about my mood as well as my nights, and we made a plan together. I kept the curtains and the steady alarm; they turned out to be part of it. Looking back, the brave thing wasn't pushing through. It was asking.

qa.q: What did Sabina's mind loop over at night?
qa.a: Work and Sabina's dad's retirement money.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel about booking the appointment?
qa.a: Sabina felt embarrassed, as if needing help meant failing.

qa.q: What made Sabina's final approach wise?
qa.a: Seeing a doctor once weeks of good habits had not worked, while keeping the curtains and steady alarm as part of the plan.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Simran to hear about those weeks?
qa.a: Simran likely felt concerned and wanted Sabina to stop battling alone, which is why the advice was gentle but clear.

grounding: Illustrates someone whose sleeplessness and worry last weeks despite good habits deciding to see a doctor, with the dark room and steady wake time kept as support.

passage:
Mohit threw his spoon and screamed. "No! No!"
"Mohit, stop that," Ayesha said. "Eat your khichdi nicely."
He shoved the bowl away and grabbed at her plate.
"Hey! That's rude."
Dadi looked up from the stove. "Ayesha, when did he last eat?"
Ayesha glanced at the clock. "Breakfast. The market took forever."
"He's hungry, not naughty."
Ayesha cooled a spoonful and held it out. Mohit gulped it, then another. His sobs slowed to hiccups.

qa.q: Why had Mohit gone so long without eating?
qa.a: The market took forever.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when he grabbed at Ayesha's plate?
qa.a: He was hungry and distressed, and grabbing and screaming were the only ways he could show it.

qa.q: What worked better than scolding, and why?
qa.a: Feeding him a cooled spoonful right away; a hungry toddler calms once food arrives, not after a telling-off.

qa.q: How does Ayesha read the screaming at first?
qa.a: She reads it as rudeness and scolds him, until Dadi's question makes her see he is hungry.

grounding: Shows a hungry toddler who cannot say so screaming, throwing and grabbing, and food ending the outburst faster than discipline.

passage: Creche note for Pema's family, Friday. Pema arrived late and missed our morning snack. By late morning she was snatching other children's biscuits, throwing her cup and refusing even the banana she loves. She couldn't tell us why. The book showed nothing since an early breakfast. I sat her down with fruit and rice; she ate in silence and was soon building towers again. On late days we will feed her as soon as she arrives. Vijay (creche teacher)

qa.q: What did Pema refuse even though she usually loves it?
qa.a: The banana.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she threw her cup?
qa.a: She was hungry and upset but could not say so, so the distress came out as snatching and throwing.

qa.q: What plan did Vijay make, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: To give Pema something to eat as soon as she arrives on late days; keeping food regular can stop the tantrum before it starts.

qa.q: How might the other children have been affected?
qa.a: They had biscuits snatched from them and may have felt upset or confused, not knowing Pema was just hungry.

grounding: Illustrates a hungry toddler showing need through grabbing, throwing and refusing food, and regular feeding settling her.

passage: At the community centre's after-school room, the rain had made every parent late. Five-year-old Yash had not eaten since lunch. He whined at the puzzle, kicked the table leg, then smacked his older brother Chaitanya for touching his crayons. When Chaitanya offered him half a biscuit, it snapped in two, and Yash burst into loud tears. "He's not usually like this," Chaitanya told the helper, Mrs Kamath. She didn't lecture. She fetched a banana and some crackers from the snack tin and sat Yash on a beanbag. Soon he was giggling and sharing his crayons.

qa.q: What happened to the biscuit Chaitanya offered?
qa.a: It snapped in two.

qa.q: Why did Yash burst into tears over the biscuit?
qa.a: He was very hungry, so he felt cross and overwhelmed, and a small upset felt huge.

qa.q: Why did Mrs Kamath's response work?
qa.a: She gave food and a quiet seat instead of a lecture, meeting the physical need behind the mood.

qa.q: What was the afternoon like for Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya got smacked and cried at while trying to help, yet still understood this was not how Yash usually is.

grounding: Shows a young child late for food turning whiny, hitting a sibling and crying over a broken biscuit, and a snack restoring him better than a lecture.

passage: From my balcony I, Bhavna, can see into the Mehtas' courtyard. On Tuesday their dinner ran late; Mrs Mehta was stuck on a work call. Little Deepak, five, went from singing to whining. He yanked his sister's plait, and when she yelled, he threw himself on the steps, wailing that his biscuit had broken "all wrong". Mrs Mehta began a lecture about manners, stopped, and handed him a chapati roll. Soon he was waving up at me. "Bhavna didi, look at my car!" I can't know what was in his head, but the change was hard to miss.

qa.q: Why did dinner run late on Tuesday?
qa.a: Mrs Mehta was stuck on a work call.

qa.q: What might Deepak have been feeling when he threw himself on the steps?
qa.a: He was probably hungry and miserable, so a broken biscuit felt like a disaster.

qa.q: What was wiser than the lecture, and why?
qa.a: Handing him a chapati roll; the mood came from hunger, so food settled him faster than words about manners.

qa.q: How might Deepak's sister see the evening?
qa.a: She had her plait yanked for no reason and may have felt hurt and angry, without knowing he was hungry.

grounding: Illustrates a young child whose late dinner turns him whiny and rough with a sibling, and food restoring him better than a lecture.

passage: Sports day rehearsal ran through the lunch break, and the tiffin boxes stayed in the classroom. By the last period Asif Sir noticed that Vaibhav, usually easy-going, was drumming his pencil, losing his place in the reading twice and snapping at his bench-mate, "Move your elbow or I'll move it!" A few children giggled. Asif's first thought was to send him to the back. Then he remembered Vaibhav's tiffin coming back unopened. "Vaibhav, did you get to eat?" Vaibhav shook his head, eyes on the desk. Asif let him eat his parathas quietly at the side table for a few minutes, then carried on with the lesson. The pencil went still.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav say to his bench-mate?
qa.a: "Move your elbow or I'll move it!"

qa.q: What made Asif Sir change his mind about sending Vaibhav to the back?
qa.a: He felt a flash of irritation, then concern when he remembered the unopened tiffin and guessed hunger was behind the snapping.

qa.q: What choice helped here, and why?
qa.a: Letting Vaibhav eat quietly for a few minutes; it met the physical need instead of punishing it as bad behaviour.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have felt if he had been sent to the back?
qa.a: Embarrassed and unfairly punished for something his hungry body was doing, and still unable to focus.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing an edgy, distracted, quarrelsome child and recognising a missed lunch as the cause instead of punishing him.

passage: In the art room of a Bandra school, Maria Miss watched Bhavna tear up her third drawing of the afternoon. Bhavna, nine, was usually the calm one in her group. Today she argued with Rukhsar over the glue, stared out of the window during the instructions and told Pranav his idea was "stupid". Maria remembered the lunch hall: Bhavna had pushed her dal-rice around and gone out to play after two bites. Instead of a warning, Maria knelt by her desk. "Tummy empty?" Bhavna nodded. Maria gave her a banana from her own bag and a quiet corner, and made a note to mention lunch to Bhavna's parents at pickup. By the bell, Bhavna was helping Rukhsar with the glue.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do with her dal-rice at lunch?
qa.a: She pushed it around and went out to play after two bites.

qa.q: What did Maria suspect when Bhavna tore up her drawing, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She suspected hunger rather than bad behaviour and felt concerned, remembering the barely touched lunch.

qa.q: How could Maria's note to the parents help?
qa.a: It lets the family know Bhavna is barely eating lunch, so together they can find food she will eat and not treat the edginess as bad behaviour.

qa.q: What might the afternoon have felt like for Bhavna before Maria knelt by her?
qa.a: Probably miserable and scratchy; with an empty stomach she could not settle, so she tore up drawings and snapped at her group.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher noticing a child who ate little at lunch turning edgy and quarrelsome, and treating it as hunger rather than misbehaviour.

subtype: Teen growth spurt appetite and grumpiness [Actor]
passage: Zeenat, you know how I bit your head off yesterday about the project? I've figured something out. I've shot up this year; every pair of trousers is short, and I'm hungry all the time. When dinner's late at home, I turn into a different person. Last Sunday Papa asked about my marks before we'd eaten, and I shouted that he never lets me breathe. Then I had a big plate of rajma chawal and felt human again, and embarrassed. It's the same pattern every time: empty stomach, short fuse, blaming whoever's closest. So I've started saying, "Give me a bit, I have to eat first, then we can talk." Papa actually laughed and said, "Fine, Lokesh, food first." And I keep peanuts in my bag now. So, sorry about yesterday. I was starving, and you got the worst of me.

qa.q: What does Lokesh now keep in the bag?
qa.a: Peanuts.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel after eating on Sunday?
qa.a: Lokesh felt human again but also embarrassed about shouting at Papa.

qa.q: What is useful about Lokesh's new line about eating before talking?
qa.a: It names the hunger early, so Lokesh can refuel before a hard conversation instead of blaming whoever is closest.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel hearing this?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel relieved to get an apology and an explanation, and less hurt about being snapped at over the project.

grounding: Shows a growing teenager who turns sharp when meals are late recognising the pattern and asking to eat before talking.

subtype: Teen growth spurt appetite and grumpiness [Actor]
passage: I'm Sarika, Ankita's older sister, and this year I've watched her grow out of every pair of jeans she owns. At our cousin's wedding in Jaipur, lunch kept getting pushed back for the rituals. By afternoon Ankita had rolled her eyes at Bua, told me my dupatta looked "tragic" and was sitting alone on the steps, chin on her knees. I couldn't tell if she was sad about something bigger. Then she stood up and said, quite calmly, "Sarika di, I'm not angry with anyone. I just need food before I talk to people." We found the snacks counter, and she ate a plate of samosas. Soon she was dancing with the little cousins, and she went back to say sorry to Bua.

qa.q: What did Ankita say about Sarika's dupatta?
qa.a: That it looked "tragic".

qa.q: What does Ankita's calm line suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She felt low and cranky from hunger, but was aware that it was not really anger at anyone.

qa.q: Which choice turned the afternoon around, and why?
qa.a: Ankita saying she needed food before talking and then eating; it met her body's need instead of letting the grumpiness land on relatives.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Ankita's moodiness at first?
qa.a: Sarika cannot tell whether it is sadness about something bigger, and only understands once Ankita names the hunger.

grounding: Illustrates a growing teenager getting sharp and low when a meal is delayed, then recognising it and asking to eat before talking.

passage:

passage: By late afternoon at the Hampi temple fair, old school friends Sangeeta and Naveen had been selling bangles since dawn without a break. When Sangeeta miscounted change for a customer, Naveen snapped, "Can't you do one simple thing right?" Her face went hot. She almost dropped the cash box and walked to the bus stand. Then she noticed his hands trembling as he tied a bundle, and remembered neither of them had eaten since the morning idlis. "Naveen. Food first. Then you can shout if you still want to." He opened his mouth, closed it and nodded. Over hot mirchi bajji from the next stall, his shoulders dropped. "Sorry. I was horrible." Later they sorted out the real problem: one of them would handle the cash box, the other the customers.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta and Naveen sell at the fair?
qa.a: Bangles.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling right after Naveen snapped?
qa.a: She felt hurt and humiliated; her face went hot and she almost walked off to the bus stand.

qa.q: What choice kept the argument from growing, and why?
qa.a: Sangeeta suggested food first; once both had eaten, Naveen could apologise and they could sort out the cash box calmly.

qa.q: How might the afternoon have felt for Naveen before they ate?
qa.a: He was likely shaky and on edge from hunger, which made a small mistake feel like a big one.

grounding: Illustrates a friend snapped at after a long day without food, and both pausing to eat before sorting out the real issue.
